chapter: Chicago, Ohio and Jelly Roll Morton
title: Recording at Victor's Camden studio; band members and Frazier's quip
summary: The band records in Camden under the Victor dog, with Jelly writing parts; Thomas recalls trumpeter Richardson and bassist Frazier.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: So he got ready to record in Philadelphia. And we recorded... That was one of the great deals to me,
because we recorded in the studios...the first Victor recording studio where they had the dog on top of it -- His Master's Voice.

Over in Camden. We'd drive down there to that big building they got the dog on top -- and that's where we recorded. That's where I saw him doing all his writing, you know. He'd write out the parts and play the (?).
How many pieces in the band did he have?

About six or seven, somewhere along there. I can't remember all the guys. I remember one guy was named Richardson; he was a trumpet player. [ROD ROSSITER PLAYED TRUMPET ON THE 9-7-29 DATE] The bass player was Frazier. And Frazier(?) was a guy that played in all the carnivals. And boy, the way he talked about carnivals, that was a great life. But we...none of us ever played in them... We didn't know what a carnival was. We probably went to see one, but we... And I remember Frazier was with us when they changed the size of the money. And I was so glad. I said, "Man, ain't that good. They're changing the size of the money and making it smaller." And Frazier said, "That ain't gonna make no difference to you. You ain't gonna have no more of it." I mean, he was telling the truth, but I was just
